questions.q: What specific gap does Always Encrypted close that TDE leaves open?
options: It keeps data encrypted in memory and in use, not just at rest — TDE decrypts pages into plaintext memory the moment a query touches them, but Always Encrypted only decrypts client-side
It replaces the need for TLS on the network connection
It encrypts backups more strongly than TDE does
It prevents firewall rules from being bypassed
questions.explain: Always Encrypted's defining property is that SQL Server itself never holds the key or sees the plaintext for a protected column.

questions.q: Where does encryption and decryption actually happen for an Always Encrypted column?
options: Client-side, inside an Always Encrypted-enabled driver (ADO.NET, JDBC, or ODBC) that holds the Column Encryption Key
Inside SQL Server's query engine, using the Column Master Key stored in the database
On the Azure SQL firewall, before the connection reaches the server
Inside the transaction log only, never in the data files
questions.explain: SQL Server never has the key, so even a sysadmin on the instance cannot decrypt the column's real values.

questions.q: Why can't classic Always Encrypted support a LIKE '%smith%' search on an encrypted column?
options: Because SQL Server never sees the plaintext, and neither deterministic nor randomized encryption preserves enough structure server-side for pattern matching without decrypting first
Because LIKE searches are disabled entirely once TDE is enabled
Because Column Master Keys don't support string data types
Because Always Encrypted only works with integer columns
questions.explain: Deterministic encryption only supports equality/joins; randomized doesn't even support that — any real computation needs decryption client-side.

questions.q: What does a secure enclave change about the Always Encrypted trade-off?
options: It provides a protected memory region where code running inside it can briefly access plaintext to perform richer operations, while still remaining invisible to the server operator (including the DBA) outside the enclave
It gives the DBA direct, unrestricted access to plaintext for troubleshooting purposes
It removes the need for a Column Master Key entirely
It moves all encryption and decryption to the client exclusively, eliminating server-side computation altogether
questions.explain: Secure enclaves let you keep the "even the server operator can't read this" guarantee while supporting operations classic Always Encrypted couldn't do server-side.

questions.q: What protects the Column Encryption Key in an Always Encrypted setup, and where does that protector typically live?
options: The Column Master Key, typically stored in Azure Key Vault or a local certificate store — somewhere SQL Server itself cannot reach
The TDE protector, stored inside the master database
A server-level firewall rule scoped to the client's IP
The database's transaction log backup chain
questions.explain: Keeping the Column Master Key outside SQL Server's reach is what makes the client-side-only decryption guarantee real.
